idiom_name: component structs with function-pointer vtables attached to an entity struct
implementation_notes: C has neither inheritance nor virtual dispatch, so the classic structure is written by hand: a component is a struct whose first members are function pointers (an explicit vtable, as in the kernel's file_operations) and the entity is a struct holding either named component pointers or a tag/registry plus void* slots. Because no container framework supplies the roles, ownership (who frees each component), type recovery and the update order are your code, which is exactly what makes the pattern explicit - and verbose - in C. The C99 ECS library flecs replaces the hand-written container with a world of registered components, queries and systems (ECS_COMPONENT/ECS_SYSTEM/ecs_progress) and is the practical choice once entity counts or component combinations grow.
pitfalls: A hand-written function-pointer vtable carries no type information: the entity must know the concrete component type it stores, and a generic slot list needs a tag or registry plus a cast nothing verifies.
Ownership is manual - decide whether the entity, the component or a pool frees what - and a component holding an Entity* dangles as soon as the entity is destroyed.
Mixing hand-rolled slots with an ECS library leaves two registration and ownership models in one program; pick one and keep the other out.

variants.name: Flecs world with registered components, queries and systems
variants.idiom_name: flecs ecs_world_t, ECS_COMPONENT, ecs_insert, ECS_SYSTEM, ecs_progress
variants.implementation_notes: Flecs stores components per type in archetypes, so an entity is an id plus a component set and behaviour lives in systems that match queries over component types; components must be registered before use (ECS_COMPONENT) and structural changes made while a system runs are deferred to a sync point. Choose it over hand-written slots when entity counts, query complexity or cache behaviour dominate, and keep ownership with the world rather than with individual entities.
pitfalls: Components must be registered (and forward-declared across translation units) before first use; an unregistered component id yields silent mismatches, not compile errors.
Systems run on a read-only world: adding or removing components inside a system is enqueued, so reads before the sync point do not see your own writes.
Component ids are runtime entities - deleting one removes that component from every entity that had it.
